content: The extent of tuberculosis (TB) disease is determined by various factors, including drug susceptibility testing (DST) results and other clinical considerations. Extensive TB disease is characterized by the presence of bilateral cavitary lesions or significant parenchymal damage as observed on chest radiography. In children under 15 years of age, advanced disease is typically defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiographs. This underscores the critical role of chest radiography in the diagnostic and clinical management of TB patients. The treatment regimen for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) includes an intensive phase lasting four months, which may be extended to six months if bacteriological conversion is not achieved by the end of the fourth month. This is followed by a continuation phase of five months, resulting in a total treatment duration of up to 11 months if extended. In the reviewed data, the use of bedaquiline and linezolid was limited to six and two months, respectively. A patient-centered approach is essential to ensure full adherence to treatment. Patients undergoing shorter MDR-TB treatment regimens require close monitoring through clinical and laboratory testing schedules, which have been successfully implemented in previous studies and programmatic settings, such as in South Africa. Monthly sputum smear microscopy and culture are recommended to monitor treatment response, similar to the monitoring schedule for longer regimens. Follow-up at 12 months post-treatment completion is also important to detect potential relapse, ideally using sputum culture and smear. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the need to strengthen and expand access to DST, as well as to monitor and conduct surveillance for emerging drug resistance, including resistance to bedaquiline and other second-line drugs. Reliable DST for all second-line medicines in shorter regimens is critical. The GDG also highlighted the importance of pediatric formulations to ensure effective treatment for children. For longer MDR-TB regimens, all three Group A agents (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid) and at least one Group B agent (clofazimine or cycloserine/terizidone) should be included to ensure the regimen starts with at least four effective agents. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. Group C agents (e.g., ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem, amikacin or streptomycin, ethionamide or prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid) may be added if necessary to complete the regimen. Kanamycin and capreomycin should not be included in MDR-TB treatment regimens. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid are strongly recommended for inclusion in longer regimens. Clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone may also be included, though with conditional recommendations due to very low certainty of evidence. Ethambutol, delamanid, and pyrazinamide may be included in longer regimens, with delamanid recommended for patients aged three years or older. Amikacin may be used in patients aged 18 years or older if susceptibility is demonstrated and adverse reactions can be adequately monitored. Ethionamide or prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid should only be used if better options are unavailable. Clavulanic acid should not be included as a standalone agent. The total treatment duration for MDR-TB patients on longer regimens is generally suggested to be 18–20 months, with adjustments based on the patient’s response to therapy. For patients achieving culture conversion, a treatment duration of 15–17 months is suggested. If amikacin or streptomycin is included, an intensive phase of 6–7 months is recommended, with modifications based on the patient’s response. Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem are administered with clavulanic acid, which is only available in combination with amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is not considered an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. The grouping of medicines for longer MDR-TB regimens is as follows: Group A: Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Group B: Clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone. Group C: Ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem, amikacin (or streptomycin), ethionamide or prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid. The recommendations for longer MDR-TB regimens are based on evidence from individual patient data (IPD) meta-analyses, which include data from observational studies and a limited number of randomized controlled trials. The overall certainty of evidence is often graded as low or very low. The GDG reviewed data from various sources, including unpublished results from clinical trials and pediatric studies, to inform their recommendations.
